what_its_for: Azithromycin is an antibiotic used to treat certain bacterial infections, including chest infections (like pneumonia and bronchitis), ear infections, throat and tonsil infections (strep throat), skin infections, and sexually transmitted infections like chlamydia. It works by stopping bacteria from growing and multiplying. Remember, it does NOT work for viral infections like the common cold or flu.
how_to_take: Take azithromycin exactly as your doctor prescribed. You can take it with or without food, but if it upsets your stomach, try taking it with a meal or a snack. Swallow tablets or capsules whole with a full glass of water. If you have a liquid (suspension), shake the bottle well before each use and measure your dose carefully with the measuring device provided — do not use a regular kitchen spoon. Take every dose as scheduled and finish your entire course of antibiotics, even if you start feeling better before it is all gone. Stopping early can allow the infection to come back or become harder to treat.
dosing: Your dose and how long you take azithromycin depends on the type of infection being treated. A common adult dosing schedule is: Day 1 — 500 mg (two 250 mg tablets), then Days 2 through 5 — 250 mg once daily. This 5-day course is often called a 'Z-Pak.' For some infections, like chlamydia, a single one-time dose of 1,000 mg may be given. Children's doses are based on body weight. Always follow your doctor's or pharmacist's specific instructions for your prescription.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one, as this can increase your risk of side effects.
storage: Store tablets and capsules at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep them away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture — do not store in a bathroom medicine cabinet. Liquid azithromycin (suspension) should be stored at room temperature and used within 10 days — do not refrigerate it unless the label specifically says to. Throw away any unused liquid after 10 days. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking antacids that contain aluminum or magnesium (like Maalox or Mylanta) at the same time as azithromycin — if you need an antacid, take it at least 2 hours before or 2 hours after your azithromycin dose. Avoid drinking alcohol while taking this medication, as it may increase side effects and weaken your immune system's ability to fight infection. Do not share your antibiotic with anyone else, even if they have similar symptoms. Tell your doctor and pharmacist about ALL medications, vitamins, and supplements you take, because azithromycin can interact with blood thinners (like warfarin), heart medications, and other antibiotics.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor or seek medical help right away if you experience: a severe allergic reaction (hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, difficulty breathing or swallowing); severe or bloody diarrhea, stomach cramps, or diarrhea that does not go away — this could be a serious gut infection; irregular heartbeat, fast or pounding heartbeat, or chest pain — azithromycin can rarely affect your heart rhythm; yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain — these may be signs of liver problems; a new skin rash or blistering of the skin; or if your infection symptoms are not getting better after a few days or they get worse at any point.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within 1 to 2 days of starting azithromycin, but it is important to finish your full course of treatment. The antibiotic continues working in your body for several days even after you take your last dose, because it stays in your tissues at effective levels. If you do not notice any improvement after 2 to 3 days, or if your symptoms get worse, contact your doctor.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Azithromycin is generally considered safe to use during pregnancy and while breastfeeding, but always tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding so they can make the best decision for you and your baby. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects, especially heart rhythm changes. Children: Azithromycin can be used in children, but the dose is carefully calculated based on body weight — never give a child an adult dose. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as your dose may need to be adjusted or the medication may not be appropriate for you. Heart conditions: If you have a history of irregular heartbeat (arrhythmia) or a heart condition called QT prolongation, let your doctor know, as azithromycin may increase the risk of serious heart rhythm problems.
